transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. Lee. To start, can you tell me what's been bringing you in to see me today?

I came in because I can’t seem to stop starting projects. Work plans, certification schedules, upgrading the home network, reaching out to old contacts—it just keeps building. I push way past normal limits until my wife or my director has to tell me to slow down.
Is this the way you've generally been for as long as you can remember, or does it feel like a distinct change from how you normally are?

It feels like a distinct change. When it happens, I start launching all these projects at once—work plans, certifications, fixing up the home network, messaging old contacts—and I just keep going until my wife or my director tells me I need to slow down.
How long has this current period of increased energy and project-starting been going on?
It’s been going on for about a year and eight months now—the stretches where I’m unusually driven and feel like I don’t need much sleep.
Have you ever had separate periods—lasting at least a couple of weeks—where you felt persistently sad, low on energy, or lost interest in things you normally enjoy?
Yeah. There are stretches where I wake up feeling like a failed version of myself—just heavy and flat. Even answering normal questions from my wife can feel like too much.
When you have one of these low, 'failed version of myself' periods, how long does it typically last—days, or two weeks or more?
They’re not just a few days. They tend to hang around for a while—more like two weeks or longer—where I feel heavy and like I’ve failed at everything.
Between these high-energy stretches and the low, heavy periods, have there been times of at least two months where your mood felt completely normal and stable?
I’m not really sure. I haven’t kept track of it that closely.

During these high-energy stretches, has your functioning been affected so severely that it caused serious problems—like conflict at work, financial trouble, or needing hospitalization—or has it mostly stayed at a level where you were still able to manage, just more intensely than usual?

It’s caused real problems. I was put on leave after a work migration failed. At home, my wife has had to step in about my spending and the late-night work, and conversations can turn into arguments. I’ve also stopped showing up reliably for church music, climbing, and mentoring.
When you're in one of these high-energy, project-starting phases, how long does that specific stretch typically last before it shifts—less than a week, or a week or more?
It’s been going on for about a year and eight months now—the stretches where I’m really driven and barely sleeping.

During these high-energy, driven periods, have you ever experienced things like hearing voices or seeing things others don't, or had strong beliefs—like feeling you had special powers or a special mission—that others told you weren't true?

Yeah. During the most driven stretches, when I was barely sleeping and pushing these huge plans, I’d hear comments in the server noise. And I started reading hidden threats into work messages—like they were aimed at me, not just normal emails.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient reports a distinct, sustained (~20 month) period of elevated, expansive mood with decreased need for sleep, increased goal-directed activity, grandiosity (multiple simultaneous projects), impulsivity (spending, risky work behavior), and severe functional impairment (leave from work, marital conflict, abandonment of usual activities). During the most intense phase of this manic episode, he developed psychotic features—auditory hallucinations (hearing voices in server noise) and persecutory delusions (believing work emails were threats aimed at him)—which occurred exclusively during the manic phase, not during euthymia. He also endorses distinct past depressive episodes lasting ≥2 weeks with anhedonia, low energy, and feelings of failure/worthlessness, confirming a bipolar course. The presence of mood-congruent/incongruent psychotic symptoms restricted to the manic episode supports Bipolar I Disorder, current episode manic, severe, with psychotic features (F31.2), rather than schizoaffective disorder (psychotic symptoms not present outside mood episodes) or a diagnosis without psychotic features (F31.1).
